title: The Last Good King
sum: 1 Esdras opens at the high point of Judah's last century: Josiah's Passover in Jerusalem in his eighteenth year. Priests in their robes, Levites set free from carrying the ark, thousands of lambs and calves from the king and his officers, singers and gatekeepers at their posts: no Passover like it since Samuel. Then two sentences found in no Hebrew book praise Josiah's upright heart and say the judgment on Israel's sins already stood (1:21–22).

The rest of the chapter runs downhill. Pharaoh marches to the Euphrates; Josiah blocks him at Megiddo, ignoring "the words of Jeremiah the prophet," and dies. Three sons and a grandson follow, two of them for only a few months, and the book says of three of them that they did what was evil in the LORD's eyes. Nebuchadnezzar carries off the vessels, the people mock the prophets, the temple burns, and the land keeps its Sabbaths for seventy years, as Jeremiah said.
readings: Verse by verse the chapter is 2 Chronicles 35:1–36:21 in Greek, with two lines added (1:21–22) and many small changes: names, numbers, the warning given to Jeremiah instead of Pharaoh, archers turned into officers. Read this way, it is a second witness, beside the Greek translation of Chronicles itself, to how these chapters were read in Greek.
Read as the opening of a book

Read as a book of its own, the chapter sets out what the rest restores. Everything taken here comes back: the temple vessels (2:9–14), the Passover kept again by the returned exiles (7:10–15), the law read in Jerusalem (9:37–55). The book begins with a king's Passover and ends with a scribe's reading of the law.

views.O: Orthodox Bibles keep 1 Esdras beside Ezra and Nehemiah: the Orthodox Study Bible lists it in the Old Testament as 1 Ezra, and the Russian Synodal Bible prints it as 2 Ezra, one of its non-canonical books. The Orthodox Church has never officially fixed one list of Old Testament books.
views.H: Dates from outside the Bible fix the events: Josiah was killed in 609 BC, the Babylonians took Jerusalem in 597, and the city and temple were burned in 587 or 586 (W. F. Albright and Rodger Young argued for 587, Edwin Thiele for 586). Where 1 Esdras departs from Kings and Chronicles in this chapter, several of its details do not fit the history those books tell: Jeconiah for Jehoahaz (1:32), the deposed king brought "up out of Egypt" (1:36), the son named Jehoiakim (1:41), and "a year later" after a reign of three months (1:43). See the notes on each verse.
views.J: Josephus tells Josiah's death at length: Neco is going to fight the Medes and Babylonians, Josiah blocks him at 'Mendes', and Josephus blames fate; he says Jeremiah's elegy for Josiah still existed in his day (Antiquities 10.74–78). The Talmud asks why so good a king died in battle and answers, through Rabbi Yohanan, that he did not consult Jeremiah (Taanit 22b), close to what 1 Esdras 1:26 says outright.
views.S: Of the 55 verses, 2 have no parallel (1:21–22), 4 keep the wording of Chronicles word for word (1:17, 1:18, 1:20, 1:42), and the other 49 differ in some detail. The largest changes: the gifts of 1:7; 'morning' for 'cattle' (1:10); Zechariah and Eddinus for Heman and Jeduthun (1:14); Jeremiah's words for Neco's (1:26); officers for archers (1:27); Josiah climbing into his chariot himself (1:29); the names of Josiah's sons (1:32, 1:41); no relation given for Zedekiah (1:44); 'the King of their ancestors' (1:48); 'the LORD's chests' (1:51). See the notes on each verse.
views.W: Catholic and Protestant churches do not count 1 Esdras as Scripture. The Council of Trent's list names only "the first and second" books of Esdras, "the second of which is called Nehemiah," and the Church of England's Article VI puts "The Third Book of Esdras" (this book, by the Latin count) first among the books the church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners" but does not use "to establish any doctrine." English readers met this chapter in the Apocrypha of the KJV.

deep.h: Why a book about the return starts with Josiah
deep.b:
1 Esdras could have begun with Cyrus, as Ezra does. Instead it begins two generations earlier, with Josiah's Passover, and the choice shapes the whole book. Josiah's Passover is the last great feast of the first temple; the returned exiles' Passover is the first great feast of the second (7:10–15, parallel Ezra 6:19–22). Josiah tears down; Ezra rebuilds. The vessels Nebuchadnezzar takes in this chapter are counted out and sent home in the next.

The two added verses (1:21–22) explain why the fall came even after a good king: the sins of the people were already written down, and the words of the Lord had "risen up" against them. That is the same answer 2 Kings gives (2 Kings 23:26–27). Read this way, chapter 1 is the reason for everything after it: Jerusalem fell for its sins, and was given back because the Lord kept his word through Jeremiah (1:55; 2:1).

Three ancient tellings of Josiah's death answer the question of why he died in different ways. 2 Kings gives no reason (2 Kings 23:29). Chronicles says he "did not listen to Neco's words from God's mouth" (2 Chronicles 35:22): God spoke through the enemy king, and Josiah did not hear. 1 Esdras says he did not heed "the words of Jeremiah the prophet from the mouth of the Lord" (1:26). The Talmud has Rabbi Yohanan say that Josiah should have asked Jeremiah, and Rav that Neco's 'God who is with me' was his idol (Taanit 22b). Josephus blames fate (Antiquities 10.76).

Each answer guards something: Chronicles guards God's freedom to speak through anyone; 1 Esdras and the rabbis guard the idea that God speaks to Israel through his prophets; Josephus, for his part, speaks of fate. The text of 1 Esdras does not say whether its writer found 'Jeremiah' in his Hebrew copy or put the name there himself.

The book does not say where or when it was made. Bullard and Hatton's handbook calls the date uncertain, says that by one argument it could not be earlier than about 150 BC, and reports that most scholars are comfortable with the first century BC; it had to be written before Josephus used it in his Jewish Antiquities, before AD 100. Its first readers, then, read their history in Greek, in the last centuries BC. The first reader we can name is Josephus. For the return from exile he follows 1 Esdras rather than the Hebrew Ezra, in its order and many of its names, though in his own words: Cyrus "king of the habitable earth," Sanabassar, Rathumus, Beeltethmus and Semellius, and the road to "Celesyria and Phoenicia" (Antiquities 11.1–30). Each card below says what is known of how that passage was heard.

echoes: 2 Chronicles 35:1–36:21; 2 Kings 23:21–25:21; Exodus 12:1–20; Leviticus 26:34–35; Jeremiah 25:11–12; Jeremiah 29:10; Lamentations 4:20; Zechariah 12:11; Daniel 1:1–2; Daniel 9:2; Ezekiel 17:11–21

settings.to: The Levites of the Jerusalem temple
settings.when: Before the Passover in Josiah's eighteenth year (1:20)
settings.why: To set the Levites to their new work: with the ark at rest in the temple, they no longer carry it, so they are to serve the Lord and the people by slaughtering and preparing the Passover in order, by David's arrangements and Moses' command.

settings.by: The king of Egypt (Neco II, not named here)
settings.to: King Josiah, as he marches to block the Egyptian army
settings.when: 609 BC, as Pharaoh goes north to the Euphrates
settings.why: To turn Josiah aside: Pharaoh claims the Lord sent him to the Euphrates, not against Judah. In 1 Esdras the reader is told in the next verse that the real warning Josiah ignored came through Jeremiah, so Pharaoh's words become a test the king fails.
settings.readers: Josephus, retelling this scene for his readers, gives Neco's aim as "to reign over Asia," names his enemies as the Medes and Babylonians, and blames fate for Josiah's choice (Antiquities 10.74–76).

settings.by: Jeremiah the prophet; then the chief men, with women
settings.when: After Josiah's death and burial in Jerusalem (1:29), and from then on "to this day"
settings.why: To mourn the king. The verse adds that the lament was "given out as a custom, to be kept forever by the whole race of Israel," so the mourning was made a custom for the whole people, not a single funeral.
settings.readers: Josephus says Jeremiah's elegy for Josiah was "extant till this time also" (Antiquities 10.78, Whiston's translation), and the Talmud has Jeremiah begin his lament with Lamentations 4:20 (Taanit 22b).

title: The Decree and the Letter
sum: Seventy years pass between two verses. In the first year of Cyrus, the Lord rouses the Persian king to keep Jeremiah's word, and he sends a proclamation through his empire: the Lord of Israel, the Lord Most High, has made him king of the whole world and told him to build a house in Jerusalem. Heads of families, priests and Levites set out, helped by their neighbors. Cyrus hands the temple vessels to his treasurer, who hands them to Sanassar, and they go home to Jerusalem: 5,469 pieces, by a count that adds up.

Then, in the book's own order, comes trouble. Under Artaxerxes, officials in Samaria write to the king that the Jews are rebuilding a rebel city, its walls and a temple, and that if it is finished he will lose his provinces. The king searches the records, agrees, and orders a halt. The officials ride to Jerusalem with horsemen and stop the work, and the temple stands unfinished until the second year of Darius. The next chapter opens at Darius's court.
readings: Read straight through, the chapter puts Artaxerxes between Cyrus and Darius, which does not match the order of the Persian kings. Josephus noticed and changed the king to Cambyses (Antiquities 11.21). Read this way, the chapter is a historical puzzle.
Read as the setup for chapters 3–4

Read as story, the halt is needed: it leaves the temple unbuilt, so that a young guard at Darius's court can win the king's leave to finish it (4:42–57). Ezra's aside about later opposition becomes the problem that the book's own court tale solves.

views.O: Orthodox Bibles keep 1 Esdras beside Ezra and Nehemiah: the Orthodox Study Bible lists it in the Old Testament as 1 Ezra, and the Russian Synodal Bible prints it as 2 Ezra, one of its non-canonical books. The Orthodox Church has never officially fixed one list of Old Testament books.
views.H: Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC; the second year of Darius I, when Haggai preached and the work began again, is 520 BC (Haggai 1:1), and the rebuilt temple was ready for use in 516. Bullard and Hatton's handbook takes the Artaxerxes of the letter as Artaxerxes I (465–424 BC) and points out that the book goes from Cyrus forward to Artaxerxes and then back to Darius. The Persian kings ran Cyrus, Cambyses, Darius I, Xerxes, Artaxerxes I, so in 1 Esdras the letter stands out of time order; Ezra too sets it "in the days of Artaxerxes" (Ezra 4:7), but after Darius has already been named (Ezra 4:5). 'Coele-Syria and Phoenicia' for 'Beyond the River' is the name the region had under the Greek kings (see the note on 2:20).
views.J: Josephus follows 1 Esdras here, not the Hebrew Ezra: his Cyrus is king of 'the habitable earth,' his vessel-keeper is Sanabassar, his officials are Rathumus, Beeltethmus and Semellius, and their letter speaks of the temple and of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia. He only changes the king's name, to Cambyses, and adds that Cyrus had read Isaiah's prophecy about him (Antiquities 11.1–30).
views.S: All 25 verses have a parallel: 2:1–14 in Ezra 1 and 2:15–25 in Ezra 4:7–24. None keeps the Plain of Ezra word for word; 2:2 differs only in 'king of the Persians' for 'king of Persia.' The main differences: the titles of God in the decree (2:3, 2:5); the heads of families 'set things in order' in Vaticanus, where Ezra has 'rose up' (2:7, see the variant); horses among the gifts (2:6, 2:8); a list of vessels whose numbers add up (2:12–13); a title read as a name (Beeltethmus, 2:15); the temple added to the letter (2:17–18, 2:25); 'Coele-Syria and Phoenicia' for 'Beyond the River'; no 'until I give the order' (2:24). Above all, the letter comes before Darius instead of after him.
views.W: Western churches hold Ezra 1 and 4 as Scripture and read these events there. 1 Esdras is printed in their Bibles, if at all, among the Apocrypha, as in the KJV, or as 3 Esdras outside the Latin canon, since Trent's list names only two books of Esdras (Ezra and Nehemiah).

deep.b:
Ezra 4 is built like a sermon on opposition, not a timeline. It starts with enemies who hinder the temple "all the days of Cyrus... until the reign of Darius" (Ezra 4:5), then jumps ahead to complaints under Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes about the city walls (Ezra 4:6–23), and then goes back: "Then the work on God's house in Jerusalem stopped" until Darius (Ezra 4:24). Read this way, Ezra 4:6–23 is an aside that gathers later troubles into one place.

1 Esdras reads the passage as a sequence. It moves the Artaxerxes letter to just after Cyrus's decree, adds the temple to the officials' complaint (2:17–18), and makes the king's reply the reason the temple work stopped (2:25). The cost is chronology: Artaxerxes now reigns before Darius. The text does not say whether 1 Esdras misread Ezra, reworked it on purpose to make room for the story of the three guards, or kept an older arrangement of the material; the book's opening pages give the views and who holds them. Josephus solved the problem in his own way by calling the king Cambyses (Antiquities 11.21).

echoes: Ezra 1:1–11; Ezra 4:7–24; 2 Chronicles 36:22–23; Isaiah 44:28; Isaiah 45:1; Jeremiah 29:10; Haggai 1:1; Nehemiah 2:1–8; Daniel 5:2–4

settings.to: The Jews in his empire, and the people living around them, by proclamation and in writing
settings.when: In the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians (2:1), who had taken Babylon in 539 BC
settings.why: To give the exiles leave to go up and build the house of the Lord of Israel in Jerusalem, and to order their neighbors to help with gold, silver, gifts, horses and livestock. For the book's readers, the pagan king's words prove Jeremiah right: the Lord, not Cyrus, ended the exile.
settings.readers: Josephus, the first reader we can name, retells the decree in its 1 Esdras form: his Cyrus says God "hath appointed me to be king of the habitable earth" (Antiquities 11.3, Whiston's translation).

settings.by: Rathymus the recorder, Samellius the scribe and their council, officials living in Samaria and the province
settings.when: Placed by 1 Esdras before the reign of Darius; in Ezra 4 it belongs to the reign of Artaxerxes I
settings.why: To persuade the king that a rebuilt Jerusalem would refuse tribute and cost him his western provinces, and so to stop the building. In 1 Esdras the complaint includes the temple, so the letter becomes the cause of the long halt.
settings.readers: Josephus read the letter in this same place, between Cyrus and Darius, and named the king Cambyses, son of Cyrus, which fits the order of the Persian kings (Antiquities 11.21).
views: 1 Esdras sets the letter between Cyrus and Darius and makes it about the temple too.
In Ezra the letter concerns the city walls in the later reign of Artaxerxes I, and is gathered into Ezra 4 as an example of opposition.

settings.to: Rathymus, Beeltethmus, Samellius and their colleagues in Samaria, Syria and Phoenicia
settings.why: To order the building stopped after a search of the records found that Jerusalem had a past of revolt and of strong kings who ruled the region. Unlike Ezra 4:21, the order leaves no room for a later change ('until I give the order').
settings.readers: In Josephus the king's reply forbids the rebuilding of "that city" (Antiquities 11.26–28), and his narrative then says the officials stopped both the city and the temple (11.29), as 1 Esdras 2:25 does.
